<reason>Side B (PRO) won the decisive clash. B's core pressure—that A's own fallback concedes public financing works for the costliest populations, leaving no principled line short of single-payer—was answered by A only with "exclusivity," and A never developed why losing alternative purchasers outweighs B's universality, administrative, and price-leverage case, especially after conceding workers have no individual exit. B also absorbed A's double-standard attack (voter fixes vs. patches) with the "repairs fund the flaw" framing, and consistently anchored the debate to the motion's actual question: whether access should track work status. A's concentration-risk route stayed live but underweighed; A never offered a positive principled defense of the work tie itself. Both sides argued cleanly without fake sourcing; B's reframes were motion-clarifying rather than evasive, and B's closing crystallized the choice more memorably.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 turn on A's continuity concession ([B2.3]-[B2.4]): showing that subsidized continuation and public fallback constitute single-payer for everyone private coverage abandons, while duplicate overhead persists. A's Rebuttal 2 answer ("exclusivity" as the principled distinction) was coherent but ultimately too thin to neutralize it, and B's closing ("identical public financing for the vulnerable, one with a redundant private roof") locked the point in.</best_rebuttal>
